blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Unit 9 (Inverse Trigonometric (TOC: 'Inverse Trigonometric Functions and Their Graphs')), arranged by the unit's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation that shows the working.
9.1 Inverse Trigonometric Functions and their Graph

blocks.prompt: 1 Which kind of function has an inverse function?

options.text: a function that is one-to-one and onto (bijective)
a function that is one-to-one only
a function that is onto only

blocks.explanation: Only a one-to-one and onto (bijective) function has an inverse: each output must come from exactly one input, and every element of the codomain must be an output.

book_ref.quote: only a one-to-one and onto function will have an inverse

blocks.prompt: 2 If \(f : X \to Y\) is bijective, then the range of \(f^{-1}\) is:

options.text: the set of all real numbers

blocks.explanation: The inverse goes from \(Y\) back to \(X\): domain of \(f^{-1}\) = range of \(f\), and range of \(f^{-1}\) = domain of \(f\) \(= X\).

book_ref.quote: is a bijective function from the set \(Y\) back to the set \(X\)

blocks.prompt: 3 The trigonometric functions are not one-to-one on \(\mathbb{R}\) mainly because they are:
blocks.explanation: They are periodic: they repeat their values at regular intervals, so many angles give the same value and the function is not one-to-one.

book_ref.quote: Due to this periodicity, trigonometric functions are generally not bijective

blocks.prompt: 4 The statement \(\frac{\pi}{3} = \sin^{-1}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) means the same as:
blocks.explanation: \(y = \sin^{-1} x\) iff \(x = \sin y\). With \(y = \frac{\pi}{3}\), \(x = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\): \(\sin\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

book_ref.quote: This means \(y\) is an angle whose sine is \(x\)

blocks.explanation: \(\sin^{-1} x\) is read 'sine inverse of \(x\)' or 'arcsine of \(x\)', written \(\arcsin x\). The other three are the reciprocal \(\frac{1}{\sin x}\).

blocks.prompt: 6 The one angle given by an inverse trigonometric function (from its restricted interval) is called the:
blocks.explanation: Restricting the domain to one standard interval leaves only one angle with the given value; that angle is the principal value.

book_ref.quote: The single angle chosen in this way is called the principal value.

blocks.prompt: 7 \(f(x) = x^{2}\) is not one-to-one on \(\mathbb{R}\). On which set is it one-to-one?
blocks.explanation: On \([0, \infty)\) different inputs give different squares. The other sets contain pairs like \(-1, 1\) with the same square \(1\).

book_ref.quote: If a function is not one-to-one, it may be possible to restrict its domain to make it one-to-one

blocks.prompt: 8 The domain of the principal sine function is:
blocks.explanation: Sine is restricted to the closed interval \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), where it increases from \(-1\) to \(1\) and takes each value once.

book_ref.quote: is called the principal sine function

blocks.explanation: The domain of the inverse is the range of the principal sine function, \([-1, 1]\).

book_ref.quote: where the domain of \(\sin^{-1} x\) is \([-1, 1]\)

blocks.explanation: \(\sin\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) and sine is odd, so \(\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\); \(-\frac{\pi}{3}\) lies in \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\). \(\frac{4\pi}{3}\), \(\frac{5\pi}{3}\) have the same sine but are outside.

book_ref.quote: This is the test for every answer

blocks.explanation: A negative input gives a negative angle: \(\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) and \(-\frac{\pi}{4} \in \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\).

book_ref.quote: are covered by the negative angles

blocks.explanation: \(\sin\frac{2\pi}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), and \(\sin^{-1}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \frac{\pi}{3}\). \(\frac{2\pi}{3}\) is outside \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), so it cannot be the answer.

book_ref.quote: must lie between \(-\frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\frac{\pi}{2}\)

blocks.prompt: 13 Which one of the following does NOT exist?
blocks.explanation: \(\sin^{-1}\) needs its input in \([-1, 1]\), and \(\frac{3}{2} > 1\). The others are defined (\(\tan^{-1}\) accepts every real number).

book_ref.quote: does not exist, because no angle has sine 2

blocks.prompt: 14 The reciprocal \(\frac{1}{\sin x}\) is equal to:
blocks.explanation: \(\frac{1}{\sin x} = \csc x\). The \(-1\) in \(\sin^{-1} x\) names the inverse function; it is not a power.

book_ref.quote: a completely different function

blocks.prompt: 15 The graph of \(y = \sin^{-1} x\) is the mirror image of the principal sine graph in the line:
blocks.explanation: Reflecting \((a, b)\) in \(y = x\) gives \((b, a)\), which is exactly how a function and its inverse are related.

book_ref.quote: So the graph of any inverse function is the reflection of the graph of the function

blocks.prompt: 16 The point \(\left(\frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{1}{2}\right)\) lies on the principal sine graph. The matching point on \(y = \sin^{-1} x\) is:
blocks.explanation: The coordinates swap: \((a, b) \to (b, a)\), so \(\left(\frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{1}{2}\right) \to \left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{\pi}{6}\right)\).

book_ref.quote: Every point \((a, b)\) of \(y = \sin x\) gives the point \((b, a)\) of \(y = \sin^{-1} x\)

blocks.prompt: 17 Besides the principal interval, sine is also one-to-one on:
blocks.explanation: On \(\left[\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3\pi}{2}\right]\) (\(n = 1\) in \(\left[n\pi - \frac{\pi}{2}, n\pi + \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\)) sine falls steadily from \(1\) to \(-1\). On \([0, \pi]\), \(\sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \sin\frac{5\pi}{6}\); on \(\left[\frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{5\pi}{4}\right]\), \(\sin\frac{\pi}{4} = \sin\frac{3\pi}{4}\).

book_ref.quote: where it is strictly increasing or decreasing, to make the sine function one-to-one

blocks.explanation: \(\sin\frac{7\pi}{6} = -\frac{1}{2}\), and the principal value of \(\sin^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\) is \(-\frac{\pi}{6}\), inside \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\).

book_ref.quote: If the interval is not specified, then

blocks.prompt: 19 The domain of the principal cosine function is:
blocks.explanation: On the closed interval \([0, \pi]\) cosine falls from \(1\) to \(-1\), taking each value once; it is one-one and onto \([-1, 1]\).

book_ref.quote: is called the principal cosine function

blocks.explanation: \(\cos\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) and \(\frac{\pi}{4} \in [0, \pi]\). \(-\frac{\pi}{4}\), \(\frac{7\pi}{4}\) have the same cosine but are outside the range.

book_ref.quote: The domain of \(\cos^{-1} x\) is \([-1, 1]\) and the range of \(\cos^{-1} x\) is \([0, \pi]\).
Some values of the principal inverse cosine

blocks.explanation: Because \(\cos(\pi - \theta) = -\cos\theta\) and \(\pi - \cos^{-1} x\) stays in \([0, \pi]\). (\(-\cos^{-1}x\) is the sine pattern and is negative, outside the range.)

book_ref.quote: A pattern you can see in the table

blocks.explanation: \(\cos\frac{4\pi}{3} = -\frac{1}{2}\); the angle in \([0, \pi]\) with cosine \(-\frac{1}{2}\) is \(\pi - \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{2\pi}{3}\).

book_ref.quote: Look at the negative inputs in the table: they give obtuse angles.

blocks.prompt: 24 Why is cosine NOT restricted to \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) to define \(\cos^{-1}\)?

options.text: cosine is even, so it is not one-to-one there

blocks.explanation: \(\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta\), e.g. \(\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \cos\frac{\pi}{4}\), so two inputs give one output. Also cosine is never negative there.

book_ref.quote: Cosine is an even function, so a negative angle and the matching positive angle always give the same value.

blocks.explanation: \(\cos^{-1}(-1) = \pi\) and \(\cos^{-1} 1 = 0\); the graph goes downward from \((-1, \pi)\) to \((1, 0)\).

book_ref.quote: A larger number has a smaller angle.

blocks.prompt: 26 Besides \([0, \pi]\), cosine is also one-to-one on:
blocks.explanation: \([\pi, 2\pi]\) is \([n\pi, n\pi + \pi]\) with \(n = 1\); cosine rises from \(-1\) to \(1\) there. In the others a pair like \(\pm\frac{\pi}{4}\) or \(\pi \pm \frac{\pi}{4}\) gives the same cosine.

book_ref.quote: or generally \([n\pi, n\pi + \pi]\)

blocks.prompt: 27 Which one of the following can NOT be a value of \(\cos^{-1} x\)?
blocks.explanation: The range of \(\cos^{-1}\) is \([0, \pi]\); a negative angle is never a value. (\(0 = \cos^{-1}1\), \(\pi = \cos^{-1}(-1)\), \(\frac{5\pi}{6} = \cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\).)

book_ref.quote: of a negative number is an obtuse angle in

blocks.explanation: \(\tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\) and \(\cos x = 0\) exactly at the odd multiples of \(\frac{\pi}{2}\).

book_ref.quote: Division by zero is not defined, so these points are not in the domain.

blocks.prompt: 29 The domain of the principal tangent function is:
blocks.explanation: It is the open interval: \(\tan\left(\pm\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) is undefined, so the end points are left out.

book_ref.quote: is called the principal tangent function

blocks.explanation: The principal tangent function takes every real value, so its inverse accepts every real number.

book_ref.quote: The domain of \(\tan^{-1} x\) is \((-\infty, \infty)\)

blocks.explanation: \(\tan\frac{\pi}{4} = 1\) and tangent is odd; a negative value gives the negative angle \(-\frac{\pi}{4} \in \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\).

book_ref.quote: Use the sign and the principal range to place the angle

blocks.explanation: \(\tan\frac{\pi}{3} = \sqrt{3}\) and \(\frac{\pi}{3} \in \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). \(\frac{4\pi}{3}\) and \(-\frac{2\pi}{3}\) have tangent \(\sqrt{3}\) too but are outside the range.

book_ref.quote: Find the reference angle from the standard values, ignoring the sign.

blocks.prompt: 33 The asymptotes of the graph of \(y = \tan^{-1} x\) are:
blocks.explanation: The vertical asymptotes \(x = \pm\frac{\pi}{2}\) of the principal tangent graph become horizontal asymptotes \(y = \pm\frac{\pi}{2}\) after reflection in \(y = x\).

book_ref.quote: the coordinates swap, so vertical lines turn into horizontal lines

blocks.explanation: \(\tan\frac{4\pi}{3} = \tan\left(\pi + \frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \sqrt{3}\), and \(\tan^{-1}\sqrt{3} = \frac{\pi}{3}\), the angle on the principal branch.

book_ref.quote: Each of these intervals is one complete branch of Figure 9.7

blocks.explanation: The range of \(\tan^{-1}\) is the open interval \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\); \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) is never reached, since \(\tan\frac{\pi}{2}\) is undefined.

book_ref.quote: Why an open interval this time (round brackets)?

blocks.prompt: 36 Which inverse function accepts every real number as its input?

book_ref.quote: taking every real value exactly once: one-to-one and onto

blocks.prompt: 37 The domain of \(\csc x\) is \(\mathbb{R}\) without the points:
blocks.explanation: \(\csc x = \frac{1}{\sin x}\), and \(\sin x = 0\) at \(x = n\pi\).

book_ref.quote: Division by zero is not allowed, so we remove every \(x\) where

blocks.explanation: \(|\sin x| \le 1\) gives \(|\csc x| \ge 1\), i.e. \((-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\).

book_ref.quote: the reciprocal always has size at least 1

blocks.prompt: 39 The domain of the principal cosecant function is:
blocks.explanation: It is the sine interval \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) with \(0\) removed, because \(\sin 0 = 0\).

book_ref.quote: called principal cosecant function

blocks.explanation: \(\csc y = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\) means \(\sin y = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), so \(y = \frac{\pi}{3}\), which is in the principal range.

book_ref.quote: A quick example of our own. Find

blocks.explanation: \(\sin y = -\frac{1}{2}\) with \(y\) in \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, 0\right) \cup \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) gives \(y = -\frac{\pi}{6}\). \(\frac{7\pi}{6}\), \(\frac{11\pi}{6}\) are outside.

book_ref.quote: Giving an answer outside \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\)

blocks.prompt: 42 Which value is never taken by \(\csc^{-1} x\)?
blocks.explanation: \(\csc 0\) is undefined, so \(0\) is not in the range \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, 0\right) \cup \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\). (\(\csc^{-1}1 = \frac{\pi}{2}\), \(\csc^{-1}(-1) = -\frac{\pi}{2}\), \(\csc^{-1}2 = \frac{\pi}{6}\).)

book_ref.quote: That is why 0 is not in the range.

blocks.prompt: 43 For which value of \(x\) is \(\csc^{-1} x\) NOT defined?
blocks.explanation: The domain of \(\csc^{-1}\) is \(\mathbb{R} - (-1, 1)\); \(\frac{1}{3}\) lies strictly between \(-1\) and \(1\).

book_ref.quote: never takes a value strictly between \(-1\) and \(1\)

blocks.prompt: 44 The domain of the principal secant function is:
blocks.explanation: It is cosine's interval \([0, \pi]\) with \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) removed, because \(\cos\frac{\pi}{2} = 0\).

book_ref.quote: is called principal secant function

blocks.explanation: \(\cos y = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) with \(y \in [0, \pi]\) gives \(y = \pi - \frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{3\pi}{4}\).

book_ref.quote: negative angles are outside the range of

blocks.explanation: \(\cos y = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) with \(y \in [0, \pi]\): \(y = \pi - \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{5\pi}{6}\). A negative answer is never possible for \(\sec^{-1}\).

book_ref.quote: Giving a negative answer for

blocks.prompt: 47 Which value is never taken by \(\sec^{-1} x\)?
blocks.explanation: \(\sec\frac{\pi}{2}\) is undefined, so \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) is not in the range. (\(\sec^{-1}1 = 0\), \(\sec^{-1}(-1) = \pi\), \(\sec^{-1}2 = \frac{\pi}{3}\).)

book_ref.quote: Including \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) in the range

blocks.prompt: 48 The horizontal asymptote of the graph of \(y = \sec^{-1} x\) is:
blocks.explanation: The vertical asymptote \(x = \frac{\pi}{2}\) of the principal secant graph becomes \(y = \frac{\pi}{2}\) after reflection in \(y = x\).

book_ref.quote: comes as close as we like to

blocks.prompt: 49 For \(x \ge 1\), the value of \(\sec^{-1} x\) lies in:
blocks.explanation: For \(x \ge 1\), \(\cos y = \frac{1}{x} \in (0, 1]\), so \(y \in \left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) (\(y = 0\) when \(x = 1\)).

book_ref.quote: For \(x \ge 1\) the values lie in

blocks.prompt: 50 The domain of the principal cotangent function is:
blocks.explanation: \(\cot x\) is undefined at \(0\) and \(\pi\); on \((0, \pi)\) it falls from \(+\infty\) to \(-\infty\), taking every real value once.

book_ref.quote: called principal cotangent function

blocks.explanation: \(\cot\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\); a negative value needs the angle in \(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right)\): \(\pi - \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{2\pi}{3}\).

book_ref.quote: become the horizontal asymptotes

blocks.explanation: On each branch \(\cot x\) falls from \(+\infty\) to \(-\infty\), so every real number is a value.

book_ref.quote: Unlike \(\csc x\) and \(\sec x\), \(\cot x\) takes every real value

blocks.explanation: \(\cot\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{\cos(\pi/2)}{\sin(\pi/2)} = 0\) and \(\frac{\pi}{2} \in (0, \pi)\). (\(0\) and \(\pi\) are not in the range.)

book_ref.quote: there is one complete branch

blocks.prompt: 56 For every inverse trigonometric function, its domain is:

options.text: the range of its principal function
the domain of its principal function
always the set of all real numbers

blocks.explanation: Domain and range swap places: the inverse's domain is the principal function's range, and its range is the principal function's domain.

book_ref.quote: each inverse function's domain is the range of its principal function

blocks.explanation: For \(x < 0\), \(\cot^{-1} x \in \left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right)\) but \(\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{x} < 0\); e.g. \(\cot^{-1}(-1) = \frac{3\pi}{4} \ne -\frac{\pi}{4}\).

blocks.prompt: 68 \(\sin^{-1} x + \sin^{-1} y\) (under the right condition) equals:
blocks.explanation: \(\sin(\alpha + \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta = x\sqrt{1 - y^{2}} + y\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}\); this is formula (i).

book_ref.quote: Inverse functions do not add like that

blocks.prompt: 69 \(\cos^{-1} x + \cos^{-1} y\) (under the right condition) equals:
blocks.explanation: \(\cos(\alpha + \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta = xy - \sqrt{1 - x^{2}}\sqrt{1 - y^{2}}\); this is formula (iii).

book_ref.quote: For a sum the sign is minus.
